findings.title: Recovery codes stored unhashed when delegated to a UserStorageProvider
findings.body: createRecoveryCodesCredential() builds the UserCredentialModel passed to user.credentialManager().updateCredential() from the raw, un-hashed `generatedCodes` list (JsonSerialization.writeValueAsString(generatedCodes), line 119/123) and hands that straight to the federated storage provider's updateCredential(). This bypasses the hashing mechanism that RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.hashRawCode()/verifyRecoveryCodeInput() implement for the local (DB) path, where only hashed codes are ever persisted via RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel. If a UserStorageProvider accepts the credential (returns true), the plaintext one-time recovery codes end up stored verbatim in the external store, unlike the hashed representation used for Keycloak's own storage. This is a security regression: anyone with read access to the external store (or its logs/backups) can recover valid one-time codes, defeating the purpose of hashing recovery codes in the first place.

findings.title: Javadoc does not document the plaintext-vs-hashed storage discrepancy
findings.body: The method's Javadoc ("Create RecoveryCodes credential either in userStorage or local storage") gives no indication that the two branches store fundamentally different representations: the user-storage branch persists raw, unhashed codes while the local-storage fallback persists hashed codes via credentialModel. This is a crucial behavioral detail for anyone implementing or reviewing a custom UserStorageProvider for this credential type, and its omission can easily lead integrators to assume codes are hashed everywhere.

findings.title: Reference test provider validates recovery codes by plaintext comparison, codifying insecure pattern
findings.body: isValid() for RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE deserializes the stored credential data and compares the raw input challenge response directly against the stored list with `generatedKeys.stream().anyMatch(key -> key.equals(input.getChallengeResponse()))`. Since this reference/test implementation (meant to illustrate correct SPI usage) stores and compares plaintext codes, it reinforces the plaintext-storage pattern introduced in CredentialHelper rather than demonstrating a secure implementation (e.g., hashing the codes itself before persisting), which real third-party storage implementers may copy.

findings.title: getCredentials() returns a live mutable reference to internal state
findings.body: credentialModels.add(myUser.getOtp()) adds the stored CredentialModel object directly (same reference held in the shared `users` map) instead of a defensive copy. Any caller that mutates the returned CredentialModel (e.g., through generic credential-management code that edits fields in place) would silently corrupt the provider's internal state for that user, since there is no copy-on-read protection. The same applies to the newly added recoveryCodes exposure path.

findings.title: New recovery-codes test does not verify stored data format/security, only functional login
findings.body: testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin() only exercises the happy-path (setup codes, log in with one). It never asserts what is actually persisted in the federated storage (e.g., whether codes are stored hashed or in plaintext), nor does it cover negative cases such as entering an invalid/used code, disabling the credential through admin/account REST, or re-authenticating after all codes are consumed when backed by a UserStorageProvider. Given the security-sensitive change to how/where codes are stored (see CredentialHelper), a test asserting the persisted representation would be valuable to catch regressions like plaintext storage.
